kicker: The Skaling law, term by term

scenes.headline: How one exponent couples model size and data
scenes.sub: FAIR's Skaling law, and the plus sign Chinchilla never tested.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Banana! Chinchilla's scaling law adds a size term to a data term. Here's why that plus sign matters, and what replaces it.

scenes.text: A sum forces the size-data interaction to exactly zero. Skaling raises the sum to one free exponent, k, so the two can interact.
scenes.say: The idea: a sum forces the size-data interaction to exactly zero. Skaling raises the sum to one free exponent, k, so they can interact.

parts.say: A over N to the alpha: model size, as in Chinchilla.

parts.note: training data, with its own independent exponent
parts.say: B over D to the beta: data, with its own exponent.

parts.note: k = 1 is Chinchilla; fitted on Farseer, k = 0.41
parts.say: Raise the sum to k. At one, it's Chinchilla. Fitted on Farseer, k is zero point four one.

parts.note: a floor the data cannot pin down
parts.say: E is the floor, which these runs can't pin down.

left.title: Chinchilla: a sum
items: A token is worth the same at any size
Saddle-shaped errors toward the grid's corners
left.say: Add two terms and the cross-derivative is zero by construction, which leaves a saddle of errors at the grid's corners.

right.title: Skaling: k below 1
items: Bigger models extract more from the same token
Loss still falls with more N or D
right.say: With k below one it turns negative: bigger models extract more from the same token.

scenes.title: Fit on an L, not the whole plane

steps.label: the full grid: every size, every budget
steps.note: Chinchilla fits it with an R squared of 0.995
steps.say: A near-perfect fit inside the grid proves little. Scaling laws are used to extrapolate.

steps.label: a row of small models, many data budgets
steps.say: So train only the cheap edges: small models across many data budgets,

steps.label: a column of small data, many model sizes
steps.note: roughly a tenth of the FLOPs
steps.say: and small data budgets across many sizes. About a tenth of the compute.

scenes.title: Error far outside the data, on Farseer
scenes.say: Fitted on that L, Skaling beats Chinchilla fitted on everything: one point five one percent error far out, against two point four six.

scenes.label: how optimal tokens per parameter trend with compute: Skaling versus Chinchilla
scenes.say: And the budget number flips sign. Model-free estimates say optimal tokens per parameter fall with compute. Skaling agrees. Chinchilla says they rise.

scenes.text: Model size and data interact. One exponent lets the law say so, and it changes where the compute should go.
scenes.say: Size and data interact. One exponent lets the law say so, and that moves where the compute should go.

recap: Chinchilla's plus sign forces zero interaction
Skaling adds one exponent; fitted k is 0.41
Fit the cheap L-shaped edges, extrapolate better
scenes.say: To recap: one plus sign, one exponent, and a cheap L-shaped grid to fit it on.
